paper_sections.title: Interaction of schizophrenia and chronic cannabis use on reward anticipation sensitivity

description.value: The study examined how schizophrenia and chronic cannabis use interactively affect behavioural and neural sensitivity to reward anticipation.

design.value: A 2 × 2 group design compared cannabis use and schizophrenia status in healthy controls and schizophrenia patients during a two-choice reward anticipation reaction-time task. Behavioural and fMRI data were analysed using reward-related contrasts, with age and education level as continuous covariates; fMRI analyses included ROI validation and between-subjects ANCOVA.

name.value: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision (ICD-10)

description.value: Patients were diagnosed by trained psychiatrists using the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision (ICD-10).
The pattern of cannabis use was defined and gathered using self-report measures, including lifetime use, duration, frequency and age of first use.

source_definition.value: Reward condition was the within-subject repeated measures factor with five levels.
Cannabis use was a between-group fixed factor with two levels; cannabis users were required to have used cannabis a minimum of once per week for one year within the past year.
Schizophrenia was a between-group fixed factor with two levels.
Age was used as a continuous covariate in all analyses including group effects.
Education level was used as a continuous covariate in all analyses including group effects.
Additional regressors included motion correction parameters estimated from the realignment step of the pre-processing.

task_name.value: two-choice RT task with elements of the MID and Eriksen flanker tasks

task_description.value: Participants completed the task in one session while being scanned using functional magnetic resonance imaging. They responded to a series of five arrow heads appearing for a fixed period, with their right or left index finger, in accordance with the pointing direction of the central arrowhead. The task was divided into 6 blocks of 60 trials.

instructions.value: The participant was informed that the aim of the task was to gain a maximal amount of points and in order for them to win (+) or avoid losing (−), they must respond both accurately and quickly.

stimuli.value: Only the incongruent configuration of the arrow heads was used (< < > < < or > > < > >). Preceding the stimulus, a valence cue was first presented, for a variable period (0.8, 2.8 or 4.8 s), consisting of either + (win), − (lose) or * (neutral), followed by the magnitude cue representing the amount of the upcoming reward (high: 20, low: 5, or none: 0).

instrument.value: Philips Achieva 3.0 Tesla TX MRI scanner

description.value: Functional MR images were acquired using echo-planar imaging with 2 s repetition time, 36 slices and 3 × 3 × 3 mm voxel size.

instrument.value: Philips Achieva 3.0 Tesla TX MRI scanner

description.value: A high-resolution T1 anatomical image with 1 × 1 × 1 mm voxel size was acquired for each participant.

Quality control was performed using ArtRepair. Pre-processing included spatial realignment, temporal interpolation to correct for delay in slice acquisition, segmentation using the T1 image, normalization to standard MNI space, smoothing with an 8 mm FWHM Gaussian kernel, and application of a 128 s high-pass filter.

steps.value: Temporal interpolation to correct for delay in slice acquisition
Excluding data with registered motion greater than 3 mm or 1 degree
Segmenting the images into grey and white matter and cerebrospinal fluid using the T1 image
Normalizing images to standard Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) space
Smoothing with an 8 mm full width at half maximum (FWHM) Gaussian kernel
Applying a high-pass filter with a 128 s cut off

model_type.value: general linear model (GLM) and 2 × 2 × 5 analysis of covariance (ANCOVA)

model_settings.value: Reward condition was the within-subject repeated measures factor with five levels; cannabis use and schizophrenia were between-group fixed factors with two levels each; education level and age were continuous covariates.

Valence, reward versus punishment, and magnitude contrast values for each subject were used as dependent variables; cannabis use and schizophrenia were fixed factors; years of education and age were continuous covariates.

A first-level within-subject GLM was applied separately to the valence and magnitude models. The valence model included reward (+), punishment (−) and neutral (*) regressors. The magnitude model included −20, −5, 0, +5 and +20 regressors. Motion correction parameters were additional regressors. T-contrasts measured valence, reward versus punishment and magnitude.

At the second level, one-sample t-tests were carried out for each contrast within predefined bilateral ROIs including striatum, thalamus, amygdala and insula subregions. Small volume correction was applied within the ROIs.

The main analysis assessed modulation of each contrast with cannabis use, schizophrenia status and their interaction, with years of education and age as covariates. Family-wise error correction adjusted for small volume was applied within independent ROIs at the voxel level; clusters were considered significant at FWE-corrected p < 0.05 with a minimum cluster size of three contiguous voxels.
